steps.explain: Write the expression inside the argument as \(z\) minus a fixed point.

\(\arg(z-z_1)=\alpha\) is a ray that starts at \(z_1\) (not included, since \(\arg 0\) is undefined) and makes angle \(\alpha\) with the positive real direction. Here \(z_1=1-i\), i.e. the point \((1,-1)\), and \(\alpha=-\frac\pi4\).
steps.work: \(\text{start }(1,-1)\ (\text{open circle}),\qquad\text{direction angle }-\tfrac{\pi}{4}\ (\text{down and to the right})\)

questions.stem:
Sketch the region in the complex plane where the inequalities \(1\le|z-i|\le2\) and \(\operatorname{Im}(z)\ge0\) hold simultaneously.

Clearly mark in all \(x\) and \(y\) intercepts.
questions.hint: |z − i| is the distance from (0, 1); draw circles of radius 1 and 2 about that point, then keep y ≥ 0.

steps.explain: \(|z-i|\) is the distance from \(z\) to the point \(i=(0,1)\). So \(1\le|z-i|\le2\) is a closed annulus (ring) centred at \((0,1)\) between the circles of radius 1 and 2.

questions.answer: The region is the part of the annulus centred at \(i=(0,1)\) with radii 1 and 2 (both circles included) that lies on or above the real axis. The outer circle meets the real axis at \(x=\pm\sqrt3\); the inner circle touches it at the origin. On the imaginary axis the boundary points are \(y=0\), \(y=2\) and \(y=3\) (the point \(y=-1\) is excluded because \(\operatorname{Im}(z)\ge0\)). The segment \(-\sqrt3\le x\le\sqrt3\) of the real axis is part of the boundary.

keyPoints.note: This is a ring centred at (0, 1) with radii 1 and 2; then keep only the part with y ≥ 0.

questions.stem:
In an Argand diagram \(z\) is a point on the circle \(|z|=2\).

Given that \(\arg z=\theta\) and \(0 \lt \theta \lt \frac{\pi}{2}\).

parts.stem: Draw a diagram to represent this information.
parts.hint: |z| = 2 is a circle of radius 2 about O; 0 < θ < π/2 is the first quadrant.

steps.explain: \(|z|=2\) means \(z\) is 2 units from the origin, so \(z\) lies on the circle centred at \(O\) with radius 2. It crosses the axes at \(\pm2\) and \(\pm2i\).
\(0 \lt \arg z \lt \frac\pi2\) puts \(z\) in the first quadrant. Draw \(Oz\) and mark \(\theta\) between the positive real axis and \(Oz\).

parts.answer: A circle centred at the origin with radius 2 (crossing the axes at \(\pm2\) and \(\pm2i\)), with the point \(z\) on the arc in the first quadrant, joined to \(O\), and the angle \(\theta\) marked between the positive real axis and \(Oz\).

keyPoints.note: Draw the circle of radius 2 about O and put z in the first quadrant with angle θ from the positive real axis.

parts.stem: Find, in terms of \(\theta\), an expression for \(\arg z^2\).

steps.explain: Write \(z\) in modulus-argument form.
By de Moivre's theorem the modulus is squared and the argument is doubled.
Since \(0 \lt \theta \lt \frac\pi2\), we have \(0 \lt 2\theta \lt \pi\), which is already a principal argument.

keyPoints.note: Multiplying complex numbers adds arguments, so arg(z²) = 2 arg z.

parts.stem:
Find, in terms of \(\theta\), giving brief reasons, an expression for:

(A) \(\arg(z+2)\)
parts.hint: z + 2 is the diagonal of a rhombus with sides z and 2.

steps.explain: Add \(z\) and \(2\) as vectors: they are adjacent sides of a parallelogram with vertices \(O\), \(2\), \(z+2\), \(z\).
In a rhombus the diagonal bisects the angle between the sides. The sides from \(O\) make angles \(0\) and \(\theta\) with the real axis.

parts.stem:
Find, in terms of \(\theta\), giving brief reasons, an expression for:

(C) \(\left|\frac{z-2}{z+2}\right|\)
parts.hint: The diagonals z + 2 and z − 2 of the rhombus are perpendicular.

steps.explain: From (A) and (B), the angle between \(z+2\) and \(z-2\) is a right angle. These are the two diagonals of the rhombus, and the diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular.
